title: A fact is a receipt line

beats.say: What is the one table every company ends up with the most rows in? It's the record of things that happened.

show.sub: the biggest table in the company

beats.say: Think of a shop receipt. Each line says who bought, what they bought, where, when, and how they paid. Then come the numbers: how many, and how much. That receipt line is a fact row. A fact is just one thing that happened, written down once.

chip.text: One thing that happened, written once

beats.say: Not every number can be added up. Fares add up fine. But a percentage, like cancellation rate, does not. Ten percent on a quiet Monday and thirty percent on a busy Tuesday is not twenty percent overall. So keep the counts, and work out the percentage last.

check.q: Why should a table keep cancelled trips and total trips instead of only a cancellation percentage?
opts: You can add the counts first and divide last
check.why: Counts add up correctly across days or cities, so you compute the true percentage after adding. Percentages from different groups cannot simply be averaged.

work: List the percentage columns in one of your tables and check that the counts behind them are stored.
Write one sentence that says what a single row in your biggest table means.

title: Grain and three kinds of measure

beats.say: A city has 100 trips over two days. How do you report the cancellation rate without getting it wrong?

First, declare the grain: one row per trip. Each row holds keys for rider, driver, city, date and payment method, plus measures like fare and distance. Fare and distance are additive, so you can sum them across any dimension.
Open trips at six p.m. are semi-additive. Add them across drivers, but not across days; take the last value or an average. Ratios are non-additive, so store cancelled trips and total trips instead.

show.title: Three kinds of measure
items: Semi-additive: sum across drivers, not days
Non-additive: ratios, store numerator and denominator

beats.say: Monday had 2 of 10 cancelled, twenty percent. Tuesday: 40 of 90, forty-four percent. Averaging the rates gives thirty-two. The true rate is 42 of 100, forty-two percent.

check.q: Monday has 2 cancelled of 10 trips. Tuesday has 40 of 90. What is the correct two-day rate?
check.why: Add numerators and denominators first: 42 over 100. Averaging the daily rates ignores that Tuesday has far more trips.

work: Write the grain of your main fact table as one sentence starting with 'One row per'.
Tag each measure as additive, semi-additive or non-additive in your docs.

title: Why the revenue is too high

beats.say: Your revenue dashboard is ten percent too high, yet every query looks correct. Why?

Often the grain is mixed. Say each trip row is repeated once per payment split. A trip paid with two cards appears twice, so its fare is counted twice. Declare one grain per table, and test that the trip key is unique.

chip.text: Test: trip key must be unique

beats.say: Balances are another trap. Adding a balance across days gives a number that means nothing. Take the end of day value instead. Averaging daily averages is also wrong, because a quiet day then counts as much as a busy one.

show.title: Aggregation traps
items: Use end of day value or an average

beats.say: Last, retries. A replayed event loads twice and inflates counts. Dedupe on a stable trip id, so a rerun gives the same answer.

check.q: A fact table at trip grain has two rows for trips paid with two cards, each carrying the full fare. What happens to SUM of fare?
check.why: The fare repeats on each row, so the sum counts it once per payment split. Keep one grain per table, or put payments in their own fact.

work: Add a uniqueness test on the declared grain key of every fact table.
Make loads idempotent by deduping on a stable business id.
Audit dashboards for sums of balances or averages of averages.

title: Atomic facts, rollups, and cost

beats.say: Should you store only daily totals, since the raw fact table is huge? Usually no.

Keep the atomic fact, one row per trip. A finer grain can answer any question later. A coarser grain can never be split back apart. The cost is volume: a billion rows a day means every scan and shuffle is expensive.

So add rollups on top for dashboards. Sums and counts merge cleanly, which is why you store numerators and denominators. Distinct counts do not merge, so use sketches such as HyperLogLog, accepting a small error.
Partition the raw fact by date so queries read only the days they need. Choose the grain by the questions you must answer, not by what is easy to load.

show.title: Design rules
items: Choose grain by the questions asked
Dashboards read rollups, not raw rows

check.q: Why keep an atomic fact table even when dashboards only need daily totals?
opts: A finer grain can be rolled up, but a coarse one cannot be split
check.why: You can always aggregate fine data upward. Once data is stored coarsely, the detail is lost, so new questions cannot be answered.

work: Estimate daily row count and bytes of your largest fact and check it is date partitioned.
Build a rollup for the top dashboard and compare scan cost against the raw table.
Use sketches for distinct counts in rollups and document the error.

title: Press twice, count once

beats.say: What if pressing the same button twice could double your money? In data, that happens all the time.

show.sub: the same event, counted two times

beats.say: Imagine a mail room. A courier is not sure a parcel arrived, so he delivers it again. Now you have two identical parcels. Fixing this means deciding what counts as one parcel, then keeping just one.
Rerunning should be like setting a thermostat to twenty degrees. Do it ten times, still twenty. Not like pressing a plus button, which climbs each time.

show.title: Safe to repeat
items: Thermostat: set to 20, ten times, still 20
Plus button: ten presses, ten more

beats.say: Late postcards are the last trick. File each by the date it was written, not the day it arrived, and glance back at the last few days of mail each morning.

check.q: A courier delivers the same parcel twice. What is the right fix?
opts: Decide what identifies one parcel and keep a single copy
check.why: Retries are normal and protect against loss, so you define what counts as one item and keep one per identity.

work: Write down, in one sentence, what one row in your main table means.
Ask which of your jobs would double rows if run twice.

title: Dedupe, overwrite, trail

beats.say: A producer retried, and now your fact table has twenty-five extra rows. How do you remove them safely?

First, declare the grain, say one row per trip. Then number rows within each trip id, ordered by event time and then id, so ties always break the same way. Keep number one. One thousand rows with twenty-five repeats becomes nine hundred seventy-five.
Next, make the load rerunnable. Overwrite the partition for October twenty-first, or merge on the trip id. A plain insert would double the day on every retry.

show.title: Idempotent load
show.text:
INSERT OVERWRITE fact PARTITION (trip_date = '2026-10-21')
SELECT ... FROM deduped;
show.note: Run it once or five times, same result

beats.say: Finally, partition by event date and reprocess the last three days each run, so rows from offline phones land in the right day.

chip.text: Late rows land on event date

check.q: Why order by event time and then id inside ROW_NUMBER?
opts: So ties break the same way on every run
check.why: Without a tiebreaker, equal timestamps let the engine pick any copy, so results can change between runs.

work: Replace any plain INSERT daily load with a partition overwrite or MERGE.
Add a ROW_NUMBER dedupe on the declared grain key with a stable tiebreaker.

title: Why totals drift overnight

beats.say: Your dedupe passes today and gives different totals tomorrow. Why?
Usually ties. If two copies share the same timestamp and you order only by time, the database may pick either one. Add the id as a final tiebreaker, so the same row wins every run.
Idempotency has traps too. Delete then insert without a transaction lets readers see an empty day. A merge fed duplicates can fail or pick randomly, so dedupe the source first.

show.title: Idempotency traps
items: Delete then insert outside a transaction: readers see an empty day
MERGE with duplicate source keys: error or random match
Dedupe the source before you merge

beats.say: Late data has a limit. If phones can be a week offline but you reprocess three days, older rows are silently missed. Keep event time and ingested time, so you can measure real lateness and size the window.

check.q: Phones can be offline up to 7 days, but you reprocess a trailing 3 days. What happens to a row that is 5 days late?
check.why: The window never revisits that partition, so the row is lost without any error. Measure lateness with event and ingested timestamps.

work: Check every dedupe ORDER BY ends in a unique id.
Compute the lateness distribution from ingested minus event time and compare it to your window.

title: What correctness costs

beats.say: Reprocessing three days every night triples your compute. Is that the right price?

Partition overwrite is cheap and simple, and it is safe to rerun. Merge touches only changed rows, which wins when a partition is huge but corrections are tiny. But merge costs more per row and needs a trustworthy key.

show.title: Overwrite or merge
items: Overwrite: simple, cheap per row, rewrites whole partition
Merge: touches only changes, costs more per row
Pick merge when partitions are huge and fixes are tiny

beats.say: Size the window from measured lateness, say ninety-nine percent arriving within two days. Chase the final one percent with a weekly backfill, not a bigger nightly window.
For restatements, overwrite when consumers want current truth. For finance, append adjustment rows so the audit trail survives. Either way, publish which days changed.

show.title: Restatement policy
items: Overwrite affected partitions for current truth
Append adjustment rows for finance audit trails

check.q: Finance needs an audit trail when a source corrects last month. Which policy fits?
opts: Append adjustment rows and publish affected days
check.why: Adjustments keep the original and the correction visible, so past reports can be reproduced and explained.

work: Pick and document a restate or adjust policy per fact table.
Set the trailing window from measured lateness and schedule a weekly backfill for the tail.

title: Four ways to remember what happened

beats.say: Why does a shop keep receipts, a nightly stock count, and a parcel tracker? Because each one answers a different kind of question.
A receipt is written once per sale and never changed. That is a transaction fact. A nightly stock count writes one line per shelf per night, even if nothing sold. That is a periodic snapshot.

chip.text: Periodic snapshot: a row even when nothing happened

beats.say: A parcel tracker is one line per parcel. You fill in ordered, shipped, delivered as it moves. That is an accumulating snapshot. And a guest list just records who was present, with no amounts at all. That is factless.

check.q: A shelf is counted every night, even on nights with no sales. Which fact type is that?
check.why: One row per entity per period, whether or not anything happened, is the definition of a periodic snapshot.

work: List the tables you own and label each as one of the four types.
Find one report that sums history to get a balance and ask if a snapshot would be simpler.

title: Transactions and periodic snapshots

beats.say: How do you get a driver's wallet balance on the fifteenth, without adding up years of payments?

A transaction fact has one row per event, like each completed trip. Rows are only added, never updated. It answers how many trips happened yesterday. But a balance needs a running sum over all history.

chip.text: Good for counts. Balances need a full running sum.

beats.say: A periodic snapshot stores one row per driver per day. With ten thousand drivers, that is ten thousand rows daily, activity or not. Now the balance on the fifteenth is a single lookup.

chip.text: Balance on the 15th is one lookup

check.q: You need each driver's balance on any past date quickly. Which design fits best?
opts: Transaction fact with a running sum
check.why: A daily snapshot stores the balance directly, so no scan of all history is needed.

work: Pick one balance-like metric and check how it is computed today.
Estimate rows per day as entities times periods before building a snapshot.

title: Accumulating and factless facts

beats.say: Where do trips stall between request and pickup? One row per event makes that surprisingly hard to see.

An accumulating snapshot keeps one row per trip. It has columns for requested, assigned, picked up and completed times. As each milestone happens, you update the same row. Subtract two timestamps and you see the delay.

chip.text: Assigned to pickup: 7 minutes. That is the stall.

beats.say: Sometimes the event itself is the fact. A factless table has no measures. One row says a driver was online in a zone in an hour. Compare it with requests to find zones with drivers but no demand.

chip.text: Rows with no measure still answer questions

check.q: You want the average minutes between assigned and picked up. Which type fits?
check.why: It keeps all milestone timestamps on one row per trip, so the gap is a simple subtraction.

work: Pick a process with stages and list its milestone columns.
Find a question about absence and check if a factless table could answer it.

title: The missing zero rows bug

beats.say: A driver had no trips on Tuesday. Does your daily balance table have a Tuesday row?
If you build a periodic snapshot from activity, it will not. Quiet days vanish, so averages are wrong and charts show gaps. The balance did not become nothing. It stayed the same.
The fix is a date spine. That is a table listing every day. Cross it with every driver, then left join the activity. Quiet days get a row, with the balance carried forward or a zero.

check.q: A daily snapshot is built by grouping activity by driver and day. What goes wrong?
opts: Days with no activity have no row
Measures become null on active days
check.why: Grouping only returns days that had activity, so zero-activity days are missing. A date spine fixes it.

work: Add a test that every entity has a row for every period.
Rebuild one snapshot from a date spine and compare row counts.

title: Loading accumulating snapshots safely

beats.say: Why is an accumulating snapshot the awkward one to load?
Its rows are revisited. Each milestone is an update, not an insert. So the pipeline must be a merge keyed on trip id, or a rerun creates duplicate trips.
Milestones not yet reached stay empty, so queries must treat nulls as still in progress, not as errors. Late events can arrive out of order, so never let an older event overwrite a newer one.

show.title: Gotchas
items: Late events arrive out of order

beats.say: Factless tables have a trap too. They record what happened, so absence needs a coverage table to compare against.

show.sub: Compare against what could have happened

check.q: A load job for an accumulating snapshot is rerun after a failure. What protects you from duplicate trips?
opts: A merge keyed on trip id
check.why: Rows are updated as milestones arrive, so loading by key makes reruns idempotent.

work: Make your accumulating load a keyed merge and test a double run.
Guard each milestone update with an event time check.

title: Choosing fact types wisely

beats.say: Do you really need all four fact types for every process?
Start with transactions. They are the cheapest, append only, and the source of truth. Derive the other types from them when a question demands it.

Snapshots trade storage for fast reads. Ten thousand drivers over three years is about eleven million rows. Cheap now, but with millions of entities it grows fast. Snapshot only what is queried often, like balances.
Use accumulating snapshots only for short, bounded processes. For long or looping flows, a transaction table of status changes is safer.

show.title: Rule of thumb
items: Long or looping flow: status change events

check.q: Support tickets can reopen many times over months. Which is the safest primary model?
check.why: Looping, long-lived flows break the fixed milestone columns. Status change events capture every step and can feed derived views.

work: Keep transactions as the base layer and build snapshots as derived tables.
Estimate snapshot storage as entities times periods before approving it.

title: The notebook with no eraser

beats.say: What if your money records had no eraser at all?
Picture a notebook written in pen. Lunch, minus twelve dollars. Refund, plus twelve. Nothing is ever crossed out. Each change is a new line at the bottom.
Made a mistake? Do not erase it. Write a new line that cancels it. The wrong line stays, and so does the fix, so anyone can see what happened.
Your balance is simply every line added up. Want the balance as of last Tuesday? Add only the lines up to Tuesday. This is called a ledger.

check.q: You booked a refund of 12 by mistake. In a ledger, what do you do?
opts: Add a new line of minus 12 that cancels it
check.why: A ledger is append only. You cancel a wrong entry with a new reversing entry, so the original and the fix both stay visible.

work: Find one money table at work that gets updated in place and note what history it loses.
Ask your finance team how they correct a wrong entry today.

title: Hold, settle, dispute: a ledger in four rows

beats.say: A customer's card hold was five hundred dollars, but the final charge was four eighty. How do you record that without editing anything?
You append entries. Day one: hold, minus five hundred. Next morning: hold release, plus five hundred, then settle, minus four eighty. Each row has a transaction id, a type, an amount and a timestamp.
Balance is the sum of amount, filtered by timestamp. Sum everything up to day one at noon: minus five hundred. Up to day two: minus four eighty.
Weeks later a dispute arrives. Append plus four eighty. History stays untouched, and the balance is right again.

check.q: Entries for t42 are hold -500, release +500, settle -480. What is the balance after settle?
check.why: Sum the amounts: -500 plus 500 minus 480 equals -480. The release cancels the hold, so only the settle remains.

work: Model one payment flow as a list of typed entries with signed amounts.
Write an as-of balance query using SUM with a timestamp filter and test it on a past date.

title: Why nobody reads the raw log

beats.say: If the log is the truth, why does nobody query it for the current balance?

show.sub: so why not read it directly?

beats.say: Because current state is a fold: read every event for that account and add them up. For an account with ten million entries, that is slow on every read.

So teams keep a current-state table, with one writer, updated from the log. They add periodic snapshots, like end of day balances, so an as-of query starts from the nearest snapshot and folds only the rest.
Gotchas: a replayed message must not post twice, so give every entry a unique key. And a late event has an event time earlier than its load time, so decide which clock your as-of balance uses.

show.title: Two classic traps
items: Replays double-post: give every entry a unique key
Late events: choose event time or load time for as-of

check.q: A payment message is delivered twice by the queue. What protects the ledger from double posting?
opts: A unique entry key that rejects the duplicate
check.why: Appending is not idempotent by itself. A unique key per entry makes a replay a no-op instead of a second posting.

work: Add a unique idempotency key to every ledger entry and enforce it.
Document whether as-of reports use event time or load time.
Reconcile the current-state table against a full fold on a schedule.

title: When a ledger is worth its cost

beats.say: Should every table in your warehouse be an event sourced ledger?

show.sub: or only where it pays off

beats.say: No. Use it where audit, as-of answers and reprocessing pay for themselves: money, inventory, regulated state. You pay in storage, a fold on every read, and a second table to maintain.

show.title: Worth it, at a price
items: Use for money, inventory, regulated state
Cost: a fold on every read
Cost: a second table to maintain

beats.say: For a customer's address, nobody needs that. A simple slowly changing dimension, or an updated row with change data capture, is cheaper and easier to query.
At scale, partition the log by account and date, snapshot daily, and reconcile the current table against a full fold nightly. If they disagree, the log wins.

check.q: Which table is the best fit for a full event sourced ledger?
opts: Payment balances needing audit and as-of reports
check.why: Ledgers earn their cost where audit trails, as-of answers and safe reprocessing matter, as with money. Low-stakes attributes are cheaper with simpler history patterns.

work: List your tables and mark which truly need audit and as-of answers.
Schedule a nightly job that compares current state to a full fold.
Use slowly changing dimensions for low-stakes attributes instead of a ledger.

title: The receipt and the filing cabinet

beats.say: Picture a shop receipt that only says customer number 4471. To learn the name, you walk to a filing cabinet. Would you write the name on the receipt instead?

If you write it on, reading is fast. No walking. But every receipt is bigger. And if the customer changes their name next year, the old receipts still show the old one. Sometimes that is exactly what you want.

chip.text: Fast to read, bigger to store

beats.say: In data, the pile of receipts is the fact table. The filing cabinet is a dimension. Copying a detail onto every receipt is called denormalising. It trades space for speed, and freezes the value at that moment.

chip.text: Denormalising: copy details onto the fact

check.q: What does copying a customer's name onto every receipt in a fact table give you?
opts: Faster reads, but more storage and a frozen value
Nothing, it is the same as a dimension
check.why: Copying avoids the lookup, so reads are faster. The cost is extra space, and old rows keep the value they had when written.

work: Pick one fact table you use and list which descriptive columns it already copies in.
Ask yourself for each one: do I want the old value kept, or the newest value everywhere?

title: Doing the volume arithmetic

beats.say: Fifty million trips a day. How big is a fact table after a year, and what does one extra column cost?

Fifty million times 365 is about 18 billion rows a year. Add a 20 byte city name to each row. That is 360 gigabytes a year before compression. Repeated text compresses well, so the real bill is smaller, but it is never zero.
Now the other side. Joining 18 billion rows to a large dimension means a shuffle, where data is moved across machines so matching keys meet. That costs time and money on every query.
So you pay storage once to save compute many times. Copy a column when most queries need it. Leave it out when it is rarely used.

show.title: The rule of thumb
items: Copy it when most queries need it
Copy it when the join is huge
Leave it out when it is rarely used

check.q: 50 million trips a day, and you add a 20 byte string to the fact. Roughly how much raw extra storage per year?
check.why: 50 million times 365 is about 18 billion rows. Times 20 bytes is about 360 GB before compression.

work: Write the rows per year and bytes per row for your biggest fact before adding any column.
Compare that storage cost with the cost of the join you would avoid.

title: Frozen values and the rewrite trap

beats.say: A rider upgrades to gold today. What tier should last month's trips show?
If the tier was copied into the fact at trip time, those trips keep the old tier. That is the value at event time. You get history without keeping versions in the dimension.

The catch is corrections. Say a city name was misspelled. In a dimension, you fix one row. In a wide fact, every copy is wrong, so you rewrite billions of rows. Miss some, and the fact disagrees with the dimension.
So copy values that are frozen by nature, like the tier at trip time. Keep anything you may need to correct everywhere in the dimension, and keep the key in the fact either way.

show.title: What to copy
items: Copy: values true at event time
Keep in dimension: anything you will correct
Always keep the key in the fact

check.q: A city name typo must be fixed everywhere. Where is that easiest?
opts: In a dimension, by fixing one row
In every fact row that copied the city
In both places at once, equally easy
check.why: A dimension holds one row to fix. Copies in a fact must all be rewritten, and any missed copy disagrees with the dimension.

work: Mark each copied column in your facts as frozen at event time or correctable.
Move the correctable ones back to the dimension, or plan a backfill job for them.

title: Narrow core, wide serving layer

beats.say: Should the fact table be wide, or should you build a wide table on top of it?

show.text: Wide fact, or wide layer on top?

beats.say: Usually the second. Keep the core fact narrow, with keys and measures, as the source of truth. Then publish a wide view or table for dashboards and language models, which struggle with joins. You rebuild it when a dimension is corrected.

chip.text: Rebuild the layer, not the truth

beats.say: Know the cost levers. Columnar storage compresses repeated text well, so a city column often costs far less than 360 gigabytes. A small dimension can be broadcast to every machine, avoiding the shuffle. Only huge dimensions truly force denormalising.

show.title: Cost levers
items: Broadcast small dimensions to skip the shuffle

beats.say: Choose by measuring. Test the join cost and the rewrite cost, then pick the cheaper pain.

show.sub: Measure both, pick the cheaper pain

check.q: Dashboards and LLM tools struggle with joins, but dimensions get corrected often. What is the best design?
opts: Copy every attribute into the core fact
Keep the core fact narrow and publish a rebuildable wide layer
Force users to write the joins themselves
check.why: A narrow core stays the source of truth and is cheap to correct. The wide layer serves easy queries and can be rebuilt when dimensions change.

work: Propose a narrow core plus wide serving table for your most-queried fact.
Benchmark one query with the join and one on the wide table, and record both costs.

title: One sheet per month

beats.say: Why would you cram a whole month into a single row?
Imagine a teacher tracking attendance. One way is a separate slip of paper for every student, every day. Thirty slips for Maya in one month. Finding her attendance means hunting through a huge pile.

The smarter way is one sheet per student per month, with thirty-one little boxes, one for each day. The position of the box tells you the day. Now Maya's whole month is one sheet you pick up in one go.
Data teams do exactly this with big tables. It is called a reduced fact. The trade is that a sheet is harder to read at a glance, so you still keep the daily slips for everyday questions.

show.title: Reduced fact
items: One row per person per month
Daily values sit in a list
Harder to read, so keep daily slips too

check.q: In the attendance analogy, what tells you which day a box on the monthly sheet belongs to?
opts: A date written in each box
The position of the box on the sheet
check.why: A reduced fact stores no date per value. The position in the list is the day, so box k means day k.

work: Find one table at work where you always sum many small rows per person over a long window.
Ask yourself whether people would still need the daily detail, and plan to keep it.

title: Reduced fact mechanics

beats.say: How do you answer trips per day over ninety days, for every rider, without reading millions of rows?
A daily fact has one row per rider per day. Ninety days means ninety rows per rider, and grouping them forces a shuffle, which is moving rows across machines so matching riders meet.

A reduced fact keeps one row per rider per month. The daily trips sit in an array, like two, zero, one, zero, zero, three. Item k is day k. October for rider seven drops from up to thirty-one rows to one. Ninety days is then about three rows per rider.
Each rider is already one row, so the sum happens locally with almost no shuffle. To read days, you unnest the array with ordinality to get the day number. A job appends each new day's value.

check.q: Why does a reduced fact need almost no shuffle for per-rider aggregates?
opts: Each rider's month is already a single row, so nothing must move to meet
The query engine caches all riders in memory
check.why: A shuffle exists to bring rows of the same key together. With the days packed in one row, the data is already together.

work: Pick your most expensive long-window per-entity query and count rows scanned per entity.
Prototype a monthly array table and compare scanned bytes and shuffle size against the daily fact.

title: Where reduced facts bite

beats.say: What breaks when a late event arrives for a reduced fact?
The array is one value in one row, so you cannot just patch a day. You must read the month's array, change position k, and rewrite the whole row. Late data means rewriting that month.

Position is the only thing that says which day. So the layout is fixed to the calendar. Every array must start on the month start, and a missing day must hold zero, not be skipped, or every later day shifts by one.
Casual analysts will struggle with arrays, so keep the daily fact and expose a daily view on top. Also, a rerun that pushes onto the end would add the day twice, so set the value by position instead.

show.title: Guardrails
items: Keep the daily fact and a daily view
Set values by position, not push
Align every array to the month start

check.q: A job reruns after a failure and appends yesterday's value to the end of each array. What goes wrong?
opts: The day is counted twice and later positions shift
check.why: Position is the date. A duplicate push inserts an extra item, so the array no longer lines up with the calendar. Set by position to stay idempotent.

work: Write the array update as set position k to value, so reruns give the same result.
Add a test that every array length equals the days in its month.

title: When to choose reduced facts

beats.say: When is a reduced fact the wrong choice?

Use it for expensive long-window metrics, like ninety-day trips per rider, where the daily scan and shuffle cost dominates. Cost drops because you scan roughly thirty times fewer rows and skip most shuffles.

Do not make it your only fact. Ad hoc slicing by day, by hour, or by other dimensions gets painful, and heavy late data forces constant rewrites. Sparse entities also waste space, because an array of thirty-one zeros stores nothing useful.

show.title: Avoid when
items: Ad hoc slicing by many dimensions

beats.say: Alternatives: a plain daily fact with good partitioning and pre-aggregated weekly rollups is simpler and handles late data easily. Choose reduced facts only when measured query cost justifies the extra pipeline, and keep the daily table as the source of truth.

show.title: Decision path
items: Keep daily as source of truth

check.q: Which situation best justifies adding a reduced fact?
opts: A rarely run report over one day of data
A costly ninety-day per-rider metric that runs constantly and rarely sees late data
A table where analysts slice by hour and by many dimensions
check.why: Reduced facts pay off for repeated long-window per-entity queries. They hurt for ad hoc slicing and frequent late data.

work: Measure cost per query before building any reduced table, and write down the target saving.
Keep the daily fact as the source of truth and derive the reduced fact from it.

title: A row of 28 light switches

beats.say: How do you remember whether someone showed up on each of the last 28 days, using almost no space?
Picture a row of 28 light switches, one per day. Switch on means the person visited that day. Instead of writing a list of dates, you just glance at the row.
Each night, slide the whole row one step along and set the newest switch. The oldest one falls off the end. Computers store that row as a single small number.
Was she here this week? Look at the last seven switches. Count the lit ones for the month.

show.title: Quick questions
items: Here today? Check the newest switch
Here this week? Any of the last 7 on
Days this month? Count the lit ones

check.q: In the switch analogy, what happens to the oldest day each night?
opts: It is copied to a backup list
It falls off the end of the row

title: One integer, three activity metrics

beats.say: How can one 32-bit number answer daily, weekly and monthly active users?

show.sub: DAU, WAU, MAU in one scan

beats.say: Bit zero means active today. Bit one means yesterday, and so on up to bit twenty-seven. A user active today and three days ago has bits zero and three set, which is the number nine.

show.title: Bit k = active k days ago

beats.say: Each night, shift the number left by one, add today's flag, and mask to twenty-eight bits. That is one cheap arithmetic step per user instead of rewriting a list of dates.

Active today: bits and one is not zero. Active in last seven: bits and one hundred twenty-seven is not zero. Active days in twenty-eight: count the set bits after masking. A billion users at four bytes is four gigabytes.

show.title: Reading the bits
show.text:
L1  = bits & 1 != 0
L7  = bits & 127 != 0
L28 = bit_count(bits & (2^28 - 1))

check.q: A user has bits equal to 9 (binary 1001). Which is true?
check.why: Bit 0 is today and bit 3 is three days ago. 8 plus 1 equals 9.

title: Where the bitmask breaks

beats.say: Your bitmask says a user is inactive, but they were actually active. What went wrong?

Late events are the usual cause. The shift happens once a night, so a late event for two days ago needs you to set that old bit by hand, or rebuild from raw data. Backfills must replay days in order, because shifting twice corrupts the history.
Watch the width. A thirty-two bit integer shifted left past its limit overflows, so always mask. Thirty-two days is the ceiling; use sixty-four bits for longer windows.
Also, a bit only says active or not. You lose event counts, and the day boundary is baked in, so a timezone change means a rebuild.

items: Day boundary and timezone are fixed in

check.q: Why must a backfill replay days in order?
opts: Because each run shifts the bits, so wrong order corrupts history
Because bit_count only works on sorted data
Because masks expire after one day
check.why: The update shifts the previous state, so running days twice or out of order moves bits to the wrong positions.

title: Bitmask or something else?

beats.say: Is a bitmask always the right way to track activity at scale?
It shines for fixed windows: DAU, WAU, MAU, retention and streaks. Retention is just an AND between two days' bits. Scans touch one narrow column, so they are fast.
Storage is not the real win. A billion users as date arrays is maybe tens of gigabytes, still affordable. The win is compute and simplicity, with no array unnesting.

Skip it when you need arbitrary date ranges, counts per day, or windows beyond sixty-four days. Use a daily partitioned active table. For approximate unique counts across dimensions, consider HyperLogLog sketches.

show.title: Choose instead
items: Per-day counts: keep a numeric fact

check.q: Which need is a poor fit for a 28-bit activity mask?
opts: Total purchases per user per day
check.why: A bit only records active or not. Per-day counts need a numeric fact such as a daily aggregate table.
